DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection (Thornbury District Council)

**What the author claims:**
- The projections rest on a local pilot.
- Participation held up across houses and flats, so a single uniform service will work.
- The financial analysis is complete.
- Treatment is local at Brookfield.
- The net cost of about £490,000 is fully covered by new-burdens funding.

**Bottom line:** the pilot is good evidence and the cost arithmetic adds up. But three of the central claims are contradicted by the study's own figures:
- **Participation did not hold up in flats.** It was 21%, against 66% in houses.
- **The projection uses a 64% participation rate the pilot never produced.** The pilot's overall rate was 57%, so projected tonnage and savings are overstated.
- **Brookfield cannot take the projected tonnage.** Its contracted capacity is 1,800 tonnes; the study projects 3,290. So treatment is only partly local, and the saving on the excess is unknown.

Once corrected, the net cost is roughly equal to the £520,000 allocation, or above it depending on where the excess goes. "Fully funded" isn't established.

The vehicle order is the one decision that can't wait, and it can probably be approved now. The rest needs revising.

## What checks out

| Check | Calculation | Document |
|---|---|---|
| Participation, houses | 2,112 / 3,200 | 66% ✓ |
| Participation, flats | 168 / 800 | 21% ✓ |
| Participation, overall | 2,280 / 4,000 | 57% ✓ |
| Vehicle cost per year | 6 × £165,000 / 7 | £141,400 ✓ |
| Crew cost | 6 × 2 × £34,000 | £408,000 ✓ |
| Table 2 total | | £733,400 ✓ |
| Disposal saving | 3,290 t × £74 | £243,000 ✓ |
| Net cost | £733,400 − £243,000 | £490,400 ✓ |

The table arithmetic is sound, and the pilot design (mixed wards, weekly measurement by housing type) is good. The problems are in what the figures are taken to show.

---

## 1. Participation did not hold up in flats

The study says "participation was broadly similar across housing types". Table 1 shows **66% for houses and 21% for flats**: flats participated at about a third of the rate of houses. Flats that did take part also put out less food waste each week (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg).

So the pilot supports the opposite of the recommendation. A **uniform service is unlikely to work for flats**. About 10,400 households, a fifth of the district, would need a different approach, such as communal bins, collection points, or targeted engagement. The study should either budget for that or explain why the low rate in flats is acceptable.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot never produced

Section 3 applies a **"64% participation rate"**. That figure doesn't appear anywhere in the pilot. The pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and its housing mix (20% flats) matches the district's, so 57% is the right starting point.

| Basis | Projected tonnes a year | Saving at £74/t |
|---|---|---|
| As in study (64% × 1.9 kg) | ~3,290 | ~£243,000 |
| Pilot overall (57% × 1.9 kg) | ~2,930 | ~£217,000 |
| By housing type (houses 66% × 1.9 kg; flats 21% × 1.4 kg) | **~2,870** | **~£212,000** |

The last row is the most accurate, because it uses each housing type's own participation rate and weekly amount. On that basis, the saving is overstated by about **£31,000 a year**, and the net cost rises to about **£521,000**, slightly above the £520,000 allocation.

The pilot ran from January to June, while the service would be new. Whether participation holds steady over a full year, through summer and once the novelty has worn off, remains open.

## 3. Brookfield can only take about half of the tonnage

Section 4 says Brookfield can offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. Even the corrected projection, about 2,870 tonnes, exceeds that by roughly **1,000 tonnes**. The study's own figure exceeds it by about 1,500. Yet the savings calculation applies Brookfield's £38 gate fee to every tonne. The excess has to go somewhere:

| Where the excess goes | Effect |
|---|---|
| AD plant 46 miles away | Gate fee unknown; much longer round trips that may need extra vehicle and crew time; not costed |
| Incineration | No saving on those tonnes, and it defeats the point of collecting food waste separately |

**If only 1,800 tonnes earn the £74 saving**, the saving is about **£133,000**, the net cost about **£600,000**, and the shortfall against the allocation about **£80,000 a year**.

So "treatment is local" holds for about 60% of the tonnage. The cost of treating the rest is the largest open question in the study.

## 4. "Fully funded" rests on provisional funding and incomplete costs

- **The allocation is provisional.** The study says the Government "has indicated" funding and calls the £520,000 "provisional". It doesn't say how many years the funding lasts, whether it rises with costs, or whether it's ring-fenced. These need confirming before Cabinet treats the service as fully funded.
- **Some costs appear to be missing:**
  - The dedicated phone line and web page (Section 6) aren't in Table 2.
  - There's no supervision, management or admin cost.
  - There's no cover for crew leave and sickness: six crews and no spare.
  - It's unclear whether £34,000 per operative includes employer on-costs.
- **The up-front cash isn't shown.** Caddies are "annualised", but caddies for 52,000 households are bought in 2026–27. The study should show this initial cash requirement.

## 5. The statutory deadline

From memory, the Simpler Recycling rules required most English councils to begin weekly household food waste collections by **31 March 2026**, with transitional arrangements for some. If that's right, an April 2027 start is after the deadline unless Thornbury has a transitional arrangement. Please check the regulations and the Council's status. Section 1 should state the deadline and how the Council will meet it.

## 6. The timetable is very tight

- Vehicles arrive in **March 2027** and collections start on **5 April**, leaving no buffer for late delivery. Crew training also depends on the vehicles arriving in March.
- Caddies go to **52,000 households in the same month**.
- The Brookfield capacity contract, and any arrangement for the excess, need to be signed before April.

There should be a fallback if vehicles arrive late, such as hired vehicles or a phased start.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Satisfaction survey.** 81% of *surveyed* households rated the service good or very good. Give the response rate and say whether non-participants were surveyed. If mainly participants responded, the figure tells you little about the 43% who didn't take part, or about flats.
- **Contamination.** Under 2% contamination in spot checks is encouraging. Say how many checks were done, and whether flats were included.
- **Liners.** Only a three-month supply of liners is planned. Say whether liners are supplied after that and whether that cost is in the £88,000 line.
- **Weekly yield.** The "All" row shows 1.9 kg, but the weighted average is 1.86 kg. That's within rounding, but use the more precise figure in the projection.

---

## What is sound

- **The pilot.** Mixed wards, weekly measurement by housing type, and contamination checks at the plant make this a stronger evidence base than national averages. The author is right to emphasise it.
- **The cost lines.** Each line in Table 2 is calculated correctly.
- **The difference in disposal costs** between incineration (£112/t) and AD (£38/t) is a real and substantial saving on every tonne that goes to Brookfield.

## Settled and open

**Settled by the study's own figures:**
- Participation in flats was about a third of that in houses, not "broadly similar".
- The projection should use 57% (or the by-type rates), not 64%, which reduces tonnage to about 2,870 and the saving to about £212,000.
- Projected tonnage exceeds Brookfield's contracted capacity by about 1,000 tonnes.

**Open:**

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| Where will about 1,000 tonnes a year go, and at what cost? | A quote and haulage costing from the 46-mile plant; whether Brookfield's capacity can be raised before 2029 |
| Is the funding secure, and for how long? | Written confirmation of the amount, duration and conditions |
| What approach is needed for flats, and what will it cost? | A costed flats plan, using pilot data on what affected participation in flats |
| Is April 2027 compliant with the statutory deadline? | Check the regulations and any transitional arrangement |
| Does participation hold over a full year? | Pilot data from July 2026 onward, if collections continued |

## Recommendation

**Approve the vehicle order now.** The legal duty to collect food waste weekly is fixed, so vehicles will be needed whatever the final treatment and flats arrangements are. A December order protects the timetable.

Ask officers to return to Cabinet before April 2027 with:
1. A corrected projection.
2. A costed treatment plan covering all the tonnage.
3. A flats strategy.
4. Confirmed funding terms.
5. A complete cost table.

The service may well be affordable. But on the study's own figures, it can't be described as fully funded or as a single uniform service.
